Seeding will occur in the fall and early winter of 2012/2013 and/or fall/early winter of 2013/14.\r\n\r\nBased on past experience, availability of site appropriate seed for the southwestern Great Basin is sparse. Also due to the severity of the 2012 fire season it is expected that obtaining seed by the early winter of 2012 may not be reasonable therefore seeding may be delayed till the following year. Seed will be dispersed either by hand using a broadcast seeder or where appropriate by a drill seeder.

Objectives: The reestablishment of plant species that provide browse and cover in the area would allow for improved habitat for many wildlife species associated with sagebrush habitat types on a seasonal or yearlong basis.
Planned_Implementation: Treatment of the big sagebrush seed with a mycorrhizal fungi inoculant available on the market would be considered, as deemed necessary. Mycorrhizal fungi is a beneficial native organism of the soil that has likely been depleted or lost on the ecological sites due to disturbance. These thread-like fungi attach themselves to plant roots and help supply plants with nutrients. It allows sagebrush seedlings, as an example, to efficiently use available moisture and nutrients needed for survival to maturity.\r\nThe plan called for overseeding approximately 130 acres along the drainages (in soil inclusions which supported big sagebrush range sites prior to the disturbance) in the seeding area classified as salt desert type in Phase II, and 400 acres consisting of every fourth swath or 1/4 of the acreage of the area classified as big sagebrush type in Phase II (based on soils).
Actual_Implementation:
The Izzenhood Phase II Big Sagebrush Seeding Project began with Ken Wilkenson (BLM Wildlife Biologist) touring the site with Marty Eldridge (BLM Equipment Operator) on December 22, 2003. There was a break due to the holidays and actual seeding began on January 5, 2004. The project was done "in house&& with BLM labor, the BLM's John Deere model 7800 4WD tractor and two Gandy seeders borrowed from NDOW for this project. There was an average of 6 to 10 inches of snow covering the area throughout the project. Tire drags were pulled behind the seeders to cover the seed in the snow. There was some speculation that this might compact the seed in the snow delaying its ability to filter down and establish in the soil.
The plan called for overseeding approximately 130 acres along the drainages (in soil inclusions which supported big sagebrush range sites prior to the disturbance) in the seeding area classified as salt desert type in Phase II, and 400 acres consisting of every fourth swath or 1;4 of the acreage of the area classified as big sagebrush type in Phase II (based on soils).
The seed mix used on the project consisted of: 900 bulk pounds of Wyoming big sagebrush, 580 bulk pounds of Basin big sagebrush and 530 pounds of rice hulls (as a dispersing agent). The recommended broadcast seeding rate on a bulk pound basis was: 1.7 bulk lbs./acre Wyoming big sagebrush, 1.1 bulk lbs./acre Basin big sagebrush, and 1.0 bulk lb./acre rice hulls for a total broadcast rate of approximately 3.8 bulk lbs./acre. An additional 440 bulk pounds of the mix was treated with inoculum and was to be broadcast over section 22 at a rate of 6.8 lbs./acre. Due to a misunderstanding, it actually went on at approximately 3.4 lbs./acre. Section 26 was also seeded with the mix treated with inoculum.
There was approximately 920 lbs. of seed left over when the project area was seeded at a rate of approximately 3.4 lbs./acre. Upon investigation we noticed that the area in section 22 called for a rate of 6.8 lbs./acre which would account for approximately 540 pounds of the leftover seed. Then there was the additional 440 lbs. of seed with inoculum (which was not accounted for) bringing the expected total to 980 pounds, which would more than explain the surplus.
With the 920 lbs. left over, two of the main drainages in section 14 were seeded. We then started back over the swaths already done in section 22 to bring it up to 6.8 lbs./acre (not considering the 440 lbs. inoculum, however). At Tom Warren&$s request, after redoing only a few swaths, we moved to the large drainage in Phase I, sections 28, 32, and 33. Marty Eldridge did the main drainage with the Gandy seeders. The main fork to the east of the drainage in section 33 was broadcast by ATV. ATVs were also used to broadcast most of the drainages in sections 22, 26, 28, and 29. The ATVs used approximately 200 pounds of the same seed mix and added approx. 40 pounds Sandburg&$s bluegrass. Approximately 20 pounds forage kochia was added along with the Sandburg&$s Bluegrass to the mix broadcast by the ATVs in sections 28 and 29, in the Phase I area.
The project was completed on January 20th. Approximately 726 acres were seeded with 2,510 bulk lbs. of seed mix yielding an average rate of 3.5 bulk lbs./acre.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
1) General conservation and rehabilitation of wildlife habitat and ecological sites in the Great Basin within Nevada BLM- Elko Field Office area of responsibility. Rehabilitation would also help prevent soil erosion. The reestablishment of plant species that provide browse and cover in the area would allow for improved habitat for many wildlife species associated with sagebrush habitat types on a seasonal or yearlong basis.
2) Establishment of vegetation that would provide a &&network&& of vegetative fuel breaks to stop or slow down potentially large scale wildfires that might occur on the area in the future. Fuel breaks would help to provide protection to the remaining blocks of native vegetation in the area and would become part of the network of seeding projects on the general area completed in the last 10 years as part of rehabilitation efforts.
3) Allow a forage base for domestic livestock management options. In concert with present seedings in the area, this seeding would allow more livestock management options to help improve the condition of other rangeland areas within affected livestock grazing allotments.

The need of the proposed action is to help rehabilitate ecological sites in the Great Basin within Nevada BLM- Elko Field Office area of responsibility. The area has been negatively altered as a result of man-caused disturbances that have affected fire regimes and the function of ecological sites.
Implementation of the proposed project would ensure that cultural resources are located and evaluated within the area, contributing to the BLM&$s overall legally mandated inventory of cultural resources on all federally-managed (public) lands.

Rangeland Ecological Site: R025XY005NV Loamy 8-10 P.Z.: The reference plant
community is dominated by Wyoming sagebrush, and Thurber’s needlegrass. Reference
vegetation community composition is approximately 55% grasses, 35% shrubs, and 10% forbs.
T79-NorthBuffalo-MAR-17
Treatment: Aerially seeded with Wyoming sagebrush, Sandberg bluegrass (Poa
secunda), bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), Munro’s globemallow
(Sphaeralcea munroana), and spiny hopsage (Grayia spinose).
2017: This plot met all objectives for density of seeded species. Perennial cover exceeded
the objective of 11% by 17%, while density was 2.8, with an objective of 1.5. Sandberg
bluegrass and bluebunch wheat grass were well established. Cheatgrass was present on
site but had been reduced from aerial herbicide treatments. Invasive annuals such as
cheatgrass and tall tumble mustard seemed restricted by the extremely rocky ground.
Litter and bare ground were within reference, but soil stability was below reference. This
may degrade the soil, which could compromise stability and water infiltration. For a
photograph of line 1, see Figure 1.
2018: This is a plot that exceeded the perennial ESR objective; the perennial cover
objective was 12.5% and the plot perennial cover was measured to be 21.3%. This plot
did not meet the density objective of 0.5 plants per square meter; density was less than
0.1 target species plants per square meter. It was previously seeded with Wyoming big
sagebrush, bluebunch wheatgrass, Munro’s globemallow (Sphaeralcea munroana), spiny
hopsage (Grayia spinosa), and Sandberg bluegrass. This gravelly plot is on a slope and
primarily dominated by grasses and forbs, including cheatgrass, with scattered shrubs of
rubber rabbitbrush. For photographs, Figure 2.
2019: This plot did not pass the ESR perennial cover objective with 10.6% compared to
the 39% annual cover. The seeding density objective was met with Sandburg bluegrass and
a small amount of globemallow spread out to 8.1 plants per meter squared. This is the
third and final visit to this plot after the 2016 Marigold fire. The area is a mix of
established perennial plants and widespread cheatgrass and tumble mustered. Rubber
rabbitbrush is almost evenly spaced across the plot with well-established pockets of basin
wild rye. There was juvenile sagebrush growing infrequently between the rabbitbrush.
The interspaces were completely covered by cheatgrass and fallen and collected tall
tumble mustard. For photographs, Figure 3.
2020: No updates.
Conclusions:
The Marigold Fire failed the ESR objective but passed the density objective for recovery
post burn after the third year of monitoring. Non-native annuals are present and have become
dominate in the fire area as well as the surrounding area. Sparse Wyoming sagebrush, evenly
spaced rabbitbrush, few globe mallow, and many Sandberg bluegrass have survived the fire and
are recruiting. Recovery of pre-burn state seems unfortunately unlikely beyond a shrub state with
an annual understory.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The fire burned a cumulative total of 1,130 acres, with 441 acres of BLM-administered lands and 689 acres of private land. The fire area burned 68 acres previously in the Jungo Road fire that occurred in 1985. The fire burned 616 acres of mapped Greater Sage-Grouse Other Habitat Management Area (OHMA). The entire fire burned area is year-round pronghorn antelope habitat and 95% of the burned area is mule deer year-round habitat as defined by the Nevada Department of Wildlife. The loss of shrub cover will negatively affect these species which utilized shrubs for cover, foraging, and nesting.\r\nRice\u2019s blue (Euphilotes pallescens ricei), a BLM sensitive species butterfly, is known to occur in the area of the fire. Rice\u2019s blue is dependent on buckwheat (Eriogonum spp.) as a larval host plant. Lahontan indigobush (Psorothamnus kingii), as special status species, has been observed growing within one mile of the fire and its habitat could be threatened due to the increasing population of non-native annuals caused by the Sand Pass fire. The Sand Pass allotment composes 698 acres of the burned area and the Bloody Runs allotment composes 432 acres of the burned area. The fire area has known populations of invasive annuals including cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) and tall tumble mustard (Sysimbrium altissimum). Lack of treatment in the area could result in monocultures of cheatgrass directly after a fire.
Conditions_At_Trt_Desc: The fire burned within two United State Department of Agriculture (USDA) Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) soil map units, containing two to three soil components each. The different soil components are associated with different USDA, NRCS rangeland\r\necological site descriptions. The fire burned within Major Land Resource Area (MLRA) 24- Humboldt Area. The possible MLRA 24 rangeland ecological sites are R024XY005NV, which is a loamy site receiving 8-10\u201d precipitation annually, R024XY017NV, which is a sandy site receiving 8-10\u201d precipitation annually, R024XY058NV, which is a sandy loam receiving 8-10\u201d precipitation annually, and a dune land site receiving 8-11\u201d precipitation annually however, is not defined as an ecological site by NRCS. The soils in the fire area are identified as moderately erosive to water and wind events. The sandy nature of these soils will contribute to accelerated soil loss and deposition due to the loss of shrub and grass cover.

Objectives: Establish desirable species at 4 per square meter or more within 5 years.
Actual_Implementation: Aerial seeding was completed on 12/19/18 by Hammond Helicopter\r\nat a cost of $4.45/ac.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The three sites that were aerial seeded only had no seedlings present of seeded species, but good
return of perennials, primarily species that were seeded in previous ESR treatments. Field
bindweed was observed at the north monitoring site on Cedar Hills, but no other noxious weeds
were observed at study sites or in the surrounding area. Detailed vegetation monitoring results
are documented below.

The ESR treatments on the Stream Complex Fire still shows good recovery overall the second year following the fire. Density of perennial species for four sites is on track to meet the four-year seeding objective. Only a couple seeded forage kochia plants were found in the aerial seeded sites, but re-established perennials from previous seedings came back well. The chaining site seeded with a native/introduced mix had very few seeded species observed, with results similar to 2018.
The chained site that received the native mix had good success in 2018 with establishing seeded species, with a total species composition of 77%. That went down in 2019 to 18% in 2019. Density of perennial plants also went from 12 plants per square meter to 5. The site has almost been completely taken over by tall tumblemustard where there had previously been bare ground. Foliar cover went from 13% to 98%, with tumble mustard accounting for 80% of that.
In 2020, the density of seeded or re-established perennial species averaged an impressive 20.77 plants per square meter. Perennials have stabilized soils and appear to be competing well with cheatgrass. Relative frequency of perennial species average across the five sites was 53.32%.
No noxious weeds were observed within the ESR site, nor were any found by the SLFO Weeds crew when they monitored in June, 2020.
